title: The Board Updates Itself
eyebrow: The screen you keep open now follows the work; the fix is running on it already

questions.ask: A card now appears on its own, but seven seconds after it changes. Do I make that instant next?

options.label: Make it instant
options.say: Fix the delay next, before anything else on the board.
options.note: Small. The delay is not the new signal — that arrives in a tenth of a second. The screen asks the machine one question per card about branches and pull requests on every refresh, five hundred and sixty five of them, and its own request waits behind that queue

options.label: Seven seconds is fine
options.say: Leave the delay; spend the time elsewhere.
options.note: Costs nothing now. The queue grows with the number of cards, so the wait gets slowly worse as the board fills

questions.note: Either way the screen updates without you touching it.

content.label: What you were looking at
content.lead: The board went stale the moment you opened it and stayed that way until you reloaded.

rows: A card is created, closed or renamed
the screen changes on its own
How long until you see it

blocks.label: Why it was silent
blocks.text: The screen listened for changes to a file. Your board does not keep its cards in that file — it keeps them in a database, and has for a long time. So every card any of us wrote landed somewhere the screen was not watching, and the screen had no way to know it was out of date.

content.label: What changed
content.lead: The screen now listens to whatever actually holds your cards, instead of to one fixed filename.

items: A board kept in a database is watched at the database; a board kept in a file is watched at the file, exactly as before.

Only real card writes wake the screen. The database rewrites its own bookkeeping on a timer with nothing behind it, and that is ignored — otherwise the board would refresh itself all night for no reason.
When several of us write at once, the screen refreshes after the last of them, not the first. It used to be able to settle one write behind.
A slow self-check runs underneath as a safety net, so a lost connection costs fifteen seconds rather than a manual reload.

content.label: How I know it works
content.lead: Measured against the board you use, on the machine you use, driven through a real browser.

rows: A real card write reaches the screen
A card changes under an open page, no reload
Same, with the live connection cut
A burst of five writes settles on the last one

blocks.label: The before column is measured, not assumed
blocks.text: The same probe was run against the board before the change and produced nothing at all — the connection opened, a card was written, and no word of it ever came back. That is what makes this a cause rather than a guess.

content.label: Three things I found on the way
content.lead: Each is on the board as its own card; none of them is fixed here.

items: The screen asks about branches and pull requests once per card on every refresh. That queue, not the new signal, is the seven seconds.
A card that is deleted never leaves an open board — the screen only ever adds and updates.
A card with no title is drawn as the word undefined instead of as an untitled card.

decisions.title: The screen follows wherever the cards are actually kept
decisions.why: The old rule named one filename and so only ever worked for one kind of board. Deciding from what is really there means a board that moves house keeps working, and the file kind behaves exactly as it did.

decisions.title: The database's own housekeeping never counts as a change
decisions.why: It rewrites part of itself on a schedule with no card behind it. Counting that would refresh your board every minute forever, which is worse than the fault being fixed.

decisions.title: A burst of writes refreshes once, after the last one
decisions.why: Five of us write at the same time constantly. Refreshing on the first write and ignoring the rest is how a screen ends up one card behind and looks correct while being wrong.

decisions.title: The board now runs as a background service
decisions.why: It was a process tied to whichever terminal happened to start it, so it died with that terminal. It now survives on its own and restarts with one command. The previous version is kept alongside it in case you want it back.

decisions.title: This job's cards stay open until the work list can see across repositories
decisions.why: The board only closes a card once it finds the commit that carries it, and it looks in one place. This change lives in the board's own screen, which is a different place. Fixing that is its own job, queued behind the rewrite already under way in the same file.

next.if_nothing: I make the seven seconds instant: the screen stops asking one question per card on every refresh.
